analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier for workers to prove job discrimination using statistics alone.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in a House subcommittee from August 1989 until that Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have changed how employment discrimination cases work under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act. A worker could establish a basic case of discrimination just by showing that a protected group was significantly underrepresented in a job or benefit compared to the qualified people who applied or were eligible. The employer could only defeat the claim by proving that every part of its hiring or selection process was a genuine business necessity. It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and then to a subcommittee, and no action ever followed.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who believe they were passed over because of race, sex, religion, or national origin. Today, building a discrimination case can require detailed evidence about how an employer's process works — information the employer holds. This bill would let a worker's statistical showing stand as the basic case, shifting the burden to the employer to justify each step of its selection process.

how_it_helps.text: A worker could establish a prima facie violation of Title VII simply by showing that the protected group's representation in a position or benefit was significantly lower than among qualified applicants or eligible persons.
The employer could rebut that showing only by proving that each part of its selection process was a business necessity — placing the burden of justification on the employer rather than the worker.

analysis.who_pays: Employers. Any business facing a discrimination suit would have to open up and defend every component of its hiring and promotion process, and statistical imbalances alone could put them in court. Some of that litigation cost would likely show up in operating expenses.

drawbacks.text: Statistical underrepresentation by itself would be enough to establish a case, even with no evidence of intentional discrimination — so employers could face lawsuits over any workforce imbalance in a given role or benefit.

Placing the burden on employers to prove a business necessity for each separate step of a selection process would raise litigation costs and could push employers toward hiring by the numbers to protect themselves, a concern central to the late-1980s debate over how discrimination claims should work.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real imbalance: employers control the records and the details of their hiring processes, and the bill would have shifted the burden of explaining those details to the party that holds them. The cost is that statistics alone would open the courtroom door, exposing employers to cases built purely on workforce numbers, with the employer forced to prove out every selection step. The remedy was narrow — it changed only how a basic case is made and rebutted — but for a worker without access to an employer's internal records, that shift is the difference between a possible case and no case at all.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and Labor Committee and then to its Subcommittee on Employment Opportunities, where it sat with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Campbell of California, a Republican, introduced the bill on August 4, 1989, with 14 original cosponsors from both parties.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
On August 24, 1989, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Employment Opportunities.
No further action appears in the record; the bill never received a subcommittee or committee vote and never reached the House floor before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced discrimination suits built on workforce statistics alone are better off that the bill never moved, and the workers it was meant to help are left with the pre-existing, more demanding burden of proof.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who would have faced statistics-based suits

for.name: Tom Campbell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered 14 cosponsors from both parties.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it out — no markup, no committee vote.

against.name: House Subcommittee on Employment Opportunities
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on August 24, 1989, and took no recorded action on it.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican and cosponsorship split 11 Republicans to 4 Democrats; the record shows no stated opposition, only inaction in a Democratic-controlled committee.

industries.note: The bill would have let workers open a discrimination case with statistical evidence alone and forced employers to prove every selection step was a business necessity, raising their litigation exposure. The bill died before any of that took effect.
